drills.title: Stationary Drop Punt
drills.objective: Develop a technically sound stationary drop punt by teaching correct ball drop, body position, foot contact and follow-through before introducing movement or defensive pressure.
setup: Under 8–10: 8–10 metres apart.
Under 12–14: 10–15 metres apart.
Under 16 and above: 15–20 metres apart.
instructions: Player A begins with the football.
Player A performs a stationary drop punt to Player B.
Player B marks or gathers the football.
Player B resets before returning the kick.
Continue for the nominated time.
Swap the preferred kicking foot after several minutes if appropriate.
coachingPoints: Hold the football correctly.
Guide the ball onto the boot rather than throwing it.
Keep their head over the football.
Strike the ball with the laces of the boot.
Finish balanced.
Follow through directly towards the target.

commonErrors.error: Throwing the ball onto the boot
commonErrors.correction: Guide the football gently from the hands.

commonErrors.error: Leaning backwards
commonErrors.correction: Keep the chest over the football.

commonErrors.error: Falling sideways
commonErrors.correction: Finish balanced on the kicking foot.

commonErrors.error: Looking at the target too early
commonErrors.correction: Watch the football until contact.

commonErrors.error: Swinging across the body
commonErrors.correction: Finish with the kicking leg pointing towards the target.

regressions: Allow players to stop and reset after every kick.
Slow the pace of the activity.
Demonstrate the technique again before restarting.
successIndicators: Maintain balance throughout the kicking action.
drills.matchApplication: The drop punt is the primary kicking technique used throughout Australian Football.This drill develops the technical foundation required for:Maintaining possession.Passing to teammates.Kicking inside 50.Defensive exits.Goal kicking.General field kicking.Every advanced kicking drill in the AFCRL builds upon the skills developed in KK-001.

drills.sourceHeading: Chapter 1 – KickingLearning ObjectivesAfter completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:Understand the importance of kicking within Australian Football.Teach correct kicking technique.Identify the major types of kicks used during matches.Recognise common technical faults.Correct technical errors using appropriate coaching cues.Progress kicking from isolated technique to match execution.Modify instruction for different age groups.Determine when players are ready to progress to more advanced kicking activities.IntroductionKicking is the defining skill of Australian Football.Unlike handball, a kick can move the football over long distances, change the angle of attack, create scoring opportunities and rapidly transition the ball from defence into offence.The quality of a team's kicking often determines its ability to control possession, maintain field position and score efficiently.For this reason, kicking should receive regular attention throughout every football season.However, coaches should avoid viewing kicking purely as a technical movement.A successful kick requires the player to:Observe the game.Assess available options.Select the correct target.Execute the skill accurately.Prepare immediately for the next contest.Every kick is therefore a combination of decision making and technical execution.Both elements must be developed together.1.1 The Purpose of KickingPlayers kick for many different reasons during a football match.Examples include:Maintaining possession.Advancing the football.Changing the angle of attack.Switching play.Entering the forward line.Finding a teammate in space.Relieving defensive pressure.Creating scoring opportunities.Kicking for goal.Every kick should have a purpose.Teaching players to kick without understanding why they are kicking limits football development.1.2 The Characteristics of an Effective KickAn effective kick is one that achieves its intended outcome.Accuracy alone is not enough.Good kicking also considers:Decision making.Distance.Timing.Trajectory.Speed.Placement.The position of teammates.The position of opponents.The best kick is not always the longest kick.Often the most effective kick is the simplest one.1.3 The Major Types of KicksPlayers should gradually become competent using several different kicks.These include:Drop PuntThe primary kick used throughout Australian Football.Suitable for:Short passes.Medium-distance passes.Long-distance passes.Goal kicking.Kick-ins.The drop punt should become every player's preferred kick.Snap KickUsed primarily when:Under immediate pressure.Kicking around the body.Attempting difficult goals.Creating angle around defenders.Banana KickUsed to curve the football around an opponent.Generally reserved for experienced players.Checkside KickUseful when space or body position limits the use of a drop punt.Requires considerable practice.Torpedo PuntAlthough less common than in previous generations, the torpedo remains useful when maximum distance is required.Examples include:Defensive clearing kicks.Long kick-ins.End-of-quarter situations.Accuracy is generally reduced compared with the drop punt.1.4 Coaching PhilosophyThe drop punt should form the foundation of every player's kicking development.Young players should not spend excessive time practising advanced kicking techniques before developing a reliable drop punt.Strong fundamentals provide the platform for more advanced skills later.1.5 Teaching OrderPlayers should generally learn kicking in the following sequence:Stationary technique.↓Short targets.↓Moving targets.↓Kicking while moving.↓Passive pressure.↓Active pressure.↓Decision making.↓Game situations.Skipping stages often leads to inconsistent technique.1.6 Coaching CuesSimple coaching cues produce the best learning.Examples include:Eyes on the ball.Drop the ball onto the boot.Point your toe towards the target.Balance before power.Finish towards your target.Stay relaxed.Coaches should avoid introducing multiple cues simultaneously.1.7 Common Technical ErrorsBeginning players frequently:Throw the ball onto the boot.Drop the ball from too high.Lean backwards.Watch the target instead of the football.Swing across the body.Rush the kicking action.Each error should be corrected individually.Avoid overwhelming players with multiple technical changes at once.1.8 Age-Specific CoachingUnder 8Focus on enjoyment.Develop confidence.Encourage both feet.Do not emphasise distance.Under 10Improve consistency.Introduce moving targets.Encourage balance.Under 12Introduce pressure.Increase decision making.Develop kicking while moving.Under 14Introduce tactical kicking.Switching play.Forward entries.Defensive exits.Under 16 and AboveDevelop match execution.Pressure.Fatigue.Decision speed.Role-specific kicking.Practical ExampleA coach notices several players leaning backwards while kicking.Instead of correcting every aspect of their technique, the coach focuses on one instruction."Keep your chest over the football."After several repetitions, the players begin striking the ball more consistently.Only then does the coach introduce the next coaching point.Volunteer Coach ChecklistBefore teaching kicking:✓ Demonstrate the skill.✓ Explain why the skill matters.✓ Keep coaching cues simple.✓ Allow plenty of repetition.✓ Progress gradually.✓ Encourage both feet.✓ Praise good decisions as well as good technique.Common Coaching MistakesFocusing on distance instead of accuracy.Teaching advanced kicks too early.Giving too many coaching cues.Ignoring the player's non-preferred foot.Practising kicking without decision making.Correcting every mistake immediately.AI Decision RulesWhen recommending kicking drills:Begin with drop punt fundamentals.Match drill difficulty to player ability.Progress towards match realism.Encourage both left and right foot development.Increase decision making before increasing distance.Prioritise accuracy before power.Chapter SummaryKicking is the foundation of Australian Football.The most effective coaches understand that successful kicking combines sound technique, intelligent decision making and consistent execution under pressure.By developing players through a logical progression, coaches build footballers capable of using their kicking skills effectively in match situations.The following chapter introduces the complete AFCRL Kicking Drill Library, beginning with the most fundamental kicking activities before progressing to advanced match simulation drills.Next Chapter: Drop Punt

drills.title: High-Low Target Handball
drills.primarySkill: Controlling handball height to varied receiving targets
drills.objective: Develop the ability to adjust handball trajectory and force so the football reaches high, central and low receiving targets accurately and safely.

groundSize.description: Pairs positioned four to five metres apart within a 20-metre × 15-metre area.

equipment: Optional coloured bibs or target cards
setup: Players form pairs four to five metres apart.
One player begins as the handballer and the other as the receiver.
The receiver may present one of three targets:Hands above chest height.
Hands at chest height.
Hands between waist and hip height.
The receiver must display the target before the handball action begins.
Players complete one round with the dominant fist and one with the non-dominant fist.
Low targets must remain above knee height to encourage safe, realistic receiving.
instructions: The receiver presents a high, central or low two-hand target.
The handballer identifies the target before organising the football.
The player adjusts the contact point, striking force and follow-through to reach the nominated height.
The receiver catches the football and resets the target.
After five repetitions, players exchange roles.
Once both players have completed each target height, the receiver varies the target randomly.
The handballer scores one point when the football reaches the presented target without forcing the receiver to move their feet.
Complete a dominant-hand round followed by a non-dominant-hand round.
coachingPoints: Look at the presented hands rather than handballing automatically to chest height.
Keep the platform aligned with the receiver.
Use a slightly higher finishing line for a high target without scooping the football.
Use a direct, controlled strike for the central target.
Reduce the finishing height and force for the low target.
Maintain legal fist contact regardless of trajectory.
Avoid excessive looping ball flight.
Make every delivery catchable and appropriate to the receiver’s position.
observations: Whether players identify the target before beginning the handball.
Whether trajectory changes are created through controlled technique rather than throwing.
Whether high handballs remain within a safe receiving range.
Whether low handballs arrive above the knees.
Whether the receiver can catch the football without moving their feet.
Whether players can make the same adjustments with both fists.
Whether ball flight remains direct rather than excessively looped.

commonErrors.error: High targets cause the player to throw the football upwards.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a stable platform and create height through the striking angle and follow-through.

commonErrors.error: Low handballs bounce before reaching the receiver.
commonErrors.correction: Increase the firmness of contact and aim above knee height.

commonErrors.error: Every handball is delivered at the same height.
commonErrors.correction: Require the player to name the target height before release.

commonErrors.error: The football travels above the receiver’s head.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce force and finish towards the presented hands.

commonErrors.error: The player looks down at the football throughout the action.
commonErrors.correction: Organise the platform, then return the eyes to the target before striking.

commonErrors.error: Non-dominant handballs lose directional control.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the distance and use predictable targets before returning to random cues.

progressions: Use random target changes immediately before release.
Alternate striking hands after each repetition.
Add a fourth target slightly to the receiver’s right or left.
Increase the partner distance by one metre.
Require three successful deliveries to each target height.
regressions: Predetermine a sequence of high, central and low targets.
Reduce the partner distance to three metres.
Allow the handballer an extended pause before release.
successIndicators: Recognise the target height before release.
Adjust handball trajectory without throwing the football.
Deliver within the receiver’s safe catching range.
Maintain direct and controlled ball flight.
Reach varied targets with both hands.
Select appropriate force for the distance and height.
drills.matchApplication: Teammates rarely present identical receiving positions. A player may need to handball over an opponent’s arm, down to a teammate gathering at ground level or directly into a runner’s hands. Controlling handball height supports possession and protects the receiver.

drills.title: High-Ball Mark Under Contact
drills.primarySkill: Completing a high mark while absorbing controlled body contact
drills.objective: Develop the ability to maintain focus, reach the football at the highest safe point and secure the mark while receiving controlled contact from an opponent.

groundSize.description: Contest zones approximately ten metres long and eight metres wide.

coachingDifficulty.description: 5 – Expert jump, contact and landing-safety management

setup: Organise groups of three.
The marker begins inside a marked contest zone.
The defender starts beside or slightly behind.
The feeder stands eight to ten metres away.
The feeder delivers a controlled high football.
The defender applies controlled body contact before or during the jump but may not tunnel, push in the back or make contact above the shoulders.
Begin with bump pads if direct contact is unsuitable.
Rotate roles after three to four repetitions.
instructions: The feeder delivers a high football towards the contest zone.
The marker and defender track the flight.
The marker establishes the preferred line to the drop point.
Controlled body contact occurs as both players prepare to jump.
The marker jumps vertically or slightly towards the football.
Both hands extend to the highest safe point.
The football is secured.
The player lands with bent knees and balanced feet.
The football is protected immediately after landing.
Players rotate roles.
coachingPoints: Track the football continuously.
Establish the drop point before jumping.
Maintain a strong core and balanced base.
Absorb legal contact without leaning dangerously.
Jump towards the football rather than away from pressure.
Extend both hands and use strong thumbs.
Secure the football before landing where possible.
Land with the knees flexed.
Protect the football immediately.
Stop the activity if contact or landing becomes unsafe.
observations: Whether the marker tracks the football.
Whether the drop point is identified.
Whether both hands reach the football.
Whether the defender avoids prohibited contact.

commonErrors.error: The marker jumps before reaching the drop point.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust the feet and delay the jump until positioned beneath the football.

commonErrors.error: The player leans away from contact.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain a strong base and jump towards the football.

commonErrors.error: The arms are used to push the opponent.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the arms available for marking and use legal body position.

commonErrors.error: The marker lands with straight knees.
commonErrors.correction: Flex the knees and absorb the landing.

commonErrors.error: The football is lowered before it is secured.
commonErrors.correction: Complete strong two-hand control at the high point.

commonErrors.error: The defender contacts the marker below the legs or in the back.
commonErrors.correction: Stop the repetition and reinforce safe legal contest positioning.

progressions: Require a post-mark disposal after landing.
drills.matchApplication: High contested marks require concentration and strong body control while opponents compete for the same space. Safe jumping and landing technique are as important as the mark itself.
drills.searchTextNormalised: mk-045 high-ball mark under contact marking completing a high mark while absorbing controlled body contact develop the ability to maintain focus, reach the football at the highest safe point and secure the mark while receiving controlled contact from an opponent.

drills.title: Tackling Fundamentals Assessment Circuit
drills.objective: Assess whether players can consistently perform the fundamental tracking, approach, contact, control, release and recovery behaviours required for safe introductory tackling.

groundSize.description: Four stations occupying approximately one-quarter of an oval or an area measuring 35 metres by 30 metres.

coachingDifficulty.description: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction

setup: Construct four separate assessment stations.
Divide players evenly across the stations.
Station 1 assesses tracking, approach and breakdown position.
Station 2 assesses legal tackle-zone contact on a shield.
Station 3 assesses controlled side-on tackling against a moving partner.
Station 4 assesses corral-or-commit decision making and recovery effort.
Assign a coach or trained observer to each station.
Match players appropriately for size and contact confidence.
Use a consistent scoring scale across all stations.
Rotate groups every five to seven minutes.
instructions: At Station 1, the defender tracks an evasive attacker through a lane without contact.
The observer assesses balance, approach angle, deceleration and ability to remain within effective range.
At Station 2, the player completes three tackle contacts on a shield from each shoulder.
The observer assesses legal target placement, head position, lead-foot distance and arm wrap.
At Station 3, the player completes controlled side-on tackles against a partner moving at approximately 50 per cent speed.
The observer assesses side entry, upright control, foot movement and immediate release.
At Station 4, the defender faces live corral-or-tackle decisions against a ball carrier.
After each repetition, the attacker may release the football or continue moving so the defender must demonstrate recovery.
Each behaviour is scored:2 points: Consistently demonstrated.
1 point: Demonstrated inconsistently or with correction.
0 points: Not demonstrated or unsafe.
Any unsafe action immediately stops the repetition and requires technical correction.
Players rotate until all four stations are completed.
Coaches record an individual strength, priority improvement and recommended regression or progression for every player.
coachingPoints: Safety takes priority over speed, force and competitive outcome.
Players must remain balanced before making contact.
Contact must remain below the shoulders and above the knees.
Head position must be safely beside or behind the opponent.
Both arms should complete the wrap.
Tacklers must avoid lifting, slinging, rotating or driving opponents into the ground.
Players must release immediately on the coach’s call.
Defenders should recover quickly after a spill, missed tackle or completed action.
observations: Whether players maintain effective defensive tracking distance.
Whether approach speed is reduced before contact.
Whether players identify and contact the legal tackle zone.
Whether head placement is consistently safe.
Whether the near foot lands close to the opponent.
Whether the ball carrier remains upright.
Whether players make appropriate corral-or-tackle decisions.
Whether players produce a second defensive effort.

commonErrors.error: Player performs well on bags but loses technique against a moving partner.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce partner speed and rebuild the side-on entry sequence.

commonErrors.error: Tackler makes inconsistent high contact.
commonErrors.correction: Lower the hips earlier and visually identify the legal zone before entry.

commonErrors.error: Head position changes during live movement.
commonErrors.correction: Slow the drill and rehearse the near-foot, shoulder and head sequence.

commonErrors.error: Player reaches instead of closing space.
commonErrors.correction: Continue tracking until the near foot can arrive beside the opponent.

commonErrors.error: Tackler controls contact but fails to release.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce the whistle and release response at every station.

commonErrors.error: Defender repeatedly lunges instead of corralling.
commonErrors.correction: Return to controlled breakdown and mirror work.

commonErrors.error: Player stops after an unsuccessful effort.
commonErrors.correction: Add a mandatory recovery target after each repetition.

progressions: Increase the speed of the moving partner for players who meet all safety standards.
Add a controlled disposal attempt during the tackle.
Introduce a second attacking threat after the initial contact.
Score decision quality as well as technical execution.
Repeat the assessment later in the training cycle and compare results.
regressions: Return players to stationary tackle-bag technique.
Replace live tackling with two-handed touch pressure.
Reduce working speed and contact resistance.
Provide individual technique coaching before reassessment.
successIndicators: Track and approach with balanced footwork.
Identify and contact the legal tackle zone.
Recover into the next defensive action.
Select appropriately between corralling and tackling.
drills.matchApplication: The circuit assesses the full introductory tackling sequence required in Australian football. Players must show that they can approach safely, complete legal contact, control rather than endanger the ball carrier, release correctly and remain involved in the next phase of play.

drills.title: Small-Sided Game Fundamentals AssessmentSG-002 – Support Triangle Possession
drills.objective: Develop players’ ability to form effective support triangles around the ball carrier and maintain multiple disposal options.
setup: Mark a square playing area.
Place one two-metre scoring gate on three sides of the square.
Divide players into two teams.
One team begins in possession.
A team scores by completing a disposal through any available gate to a teammate.
instructions: The possession team moves the football inside the square.
At least two teammates must create different support angles around the ball carrier.
A point is scored when a player disposes through a gate to a teammate positioned outside the square.
The outside receiver immediately returns the football into the playing area.
The same gate cannot be used for consecutive scores.
Defenders attempt to intercept, force an error or touch the football.
Possession changes after a turnover or when the football leaves the area without passing through a gate.
Teams play two-minute rounds and attempt to record the highest score.
coachingPoints: Position one support player ahead of the ball and another behind or beside it.
Avoid placing all options on the same line.
Move early so the ball carrier can identify options before pressure arrives.
Maintain enough distance to prevent one defender covering multiple players.
Re-form the support triangle immediately after each disposal.
Communicate whether the option is forward, lateral or behind.
Defenders should close the most dangerous option while pressuring the ball carrier.
observations: Whether the ball carrier regularly has at least two visible options.
Whether support players occupy different angles and depths.
Whether defenders can cover several attackers because spacing is too narrow.
Whether the possession team scans for a new gate after scoring.

commonErrors.error: Support players stand directly behind defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Lead laterally until the ball carrier has a clear sightline.

commonErrors.error: All support players move forward.
commonErrors.correction: Assign one player to remain behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Players follow their disposal too closely.
commonErrors.correction: Require players to clear five metres before offering again.

commonErrors.error: The same gate is repeatedly targeted.
commonErrors.correction: Enforce the alternate-gate rule and reward early scanning.

commonErrors.error: Ball carriers hold the football too long.
commonErrors.correction: Introduce a three-second disposal count.

progressions: Require a kick through selected gates and a handball through others.
Allow full tackling for appropriate players.
Award bonus points when all team members touch the football before a score.
regressions: Increase the size of the square.
successIndicators: Create support on more than one side of the ball carrier.
Identify an available gate before receiving.
Retain possession despite changing defensive pressure.
drills.matchApplication: Support triangles provide the ball carrier with forward, lateral and release options during contested possession, defensive exits and open-field ball movement.

drills.title: Complete Kicking Competency AssessmentKK-150 – Complete Kicking Competency Assessment
drills.primarySkill: Comprehensive Assessment of AFL Kicking Competency
drills.objective: Provide a complete assessment of each player’s kicking technique, versatility, decision making and tactical execution across every major AFL kicking situation.

groundSize.description: Full Ground with Multiple Assessment Stations

setup: Basic drop-punt technique.
Short-kick accuracy.
Medium and long kicking.
Preferred and non-preferred foot.
Kicking on the run.
Kicking under pressure.
Goal kicking.
Defensive exit decisions.
Forward-entry decisions.
Full-ground match simulation.
instructions: Players complete each technical station.
Coaches record:Accuracy.
Distance.
Trajectory.
Ball-drop consistency.
Balance.
Preferred and non-preferred-side performance.
Players then complete decision-making stations under pressure.
Goal-kicking performance is assessed from:Set shots.
Running shots.
Snaps.
Bananas.
Tight angles.
Fatigue.
Players finish with a live match simulation.
Coaches combine all results into an individual kicking profile.
Each player receives priority development areas and recommended drills.
coachingPoints: Apply consistent technical fundamentals.
Select the correct kick for the situation.
Balance risk and reward.
Maintain execution under pressure and fatigue.
Use both sides of the body.
Communicate with teammates.
Understand personal strengths and limitations.
Transfer isolated skills into match play.

commonErrors.error: Player focuses only on kicking distance
commonErrors.correction: Assess accuracy, trajectory and tactical value as well.

commonErrors.error: Technique changes between stations
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce consistent fundamentals.

commonErrors.error: Player performs well unopposed but struggles under pressure
commonErrors.correction: Prioritise pressure-based progression drills.

commonErrors.error: Non-preferred foot is avoided
commonErrors.correction: Include regular opposite-side development.

commonErrors.error: Decision making does not match technical ability
commonErrors.correction: Use scenario-based kicking drills.

commonErrors.error: Goal-kicking routine changes under pressure
commonErrors.correction: Rebuild a repeatable routine.

commonErrors.error: Assessment results are treated as permanent
commonErrors.correction: Use results as a development baseline.

progressions: Compare results across multiple testing periods.
Use opposition pressure at every station.
Add match statistics to the assessment profile.
regressions: Assess one skill group per session.
Use larger targets for younger players.
successIndicators: Accurate short, medium and long disposal.
drills.matchApplication: Provides a complete evidence-based profile of each player’s ability to execute AFL kicking skills in technical, tactical and match-pressure environments.

drills.sourceHeading: Chapter 1 – KickingLearning ObjectivesAfter completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:Understand the importance of kicking within Australian Football.Teach correct kicking technique.Identify the major types of kicks used during matches.Recognise common technical faults.Correct technical errors using appropriate coaching cues.Progress kicking from isolated technique to match execution.Modify instruction for different age groups.Determine when players are ready to progress to more advanced kicking activities.IntroductionKicking is the defining skill of Australian Football.Unlike handball, a kick can move the football over long distances, change the angle of attack, create scoring opportunities and rapidly transition the ball from defence into offence.The quality of a team's kicking often determines its ability to control possession, maintain field position and score efficiently.For this reason, kicking should receive regular attention throughout every football season.However, coaches should avoid viewing kicking purely as a technical movement.A successful kick requires the player to:Observe the game.Assess available options.Select the correct target.Execute the skill accurately.Prepare immediately for the next contest.Every kick is therefore a combination of decision making and technical execution.Both elements must be developed together.1.1 The Purpose of KickingPlayers kick for many different reasons during a football match.Examples include:Maintaining possession.Advancing the football.Changing the angle of attack.Switching play.Entering the forward line.Finding a teammate in space.Relieving defensive pressure.Creating scoring opportunities.Kicking for goal.Every kick should have a purpose.Teaching players to kick without understanding why they are kicking limits football development.1.2 The Characteristics of an Effective KickAn effective kick is one that achieves its intended outcome.Accuracy alone is not enough.Good kicking also considers:Decision making.Distance.Timing.Trajectory.Speed.Placement.The position of teammates.The position of opponents.The best kick is not always the longest kick.Often the most effective kick is the simplest one.1.3 The Major Types of KicksPlayers should gradually become competent using several different kicks.These include:Drop PuntThe primary kick used throughout Australian Football.Suitable for:Short passes.Medium-distance passes.Long-distance passes.Goal kicking.Kick-ins.The drop punt should become every player's preferred kick.Snap KickUsed primarily when:Under immediate pressure.Kicking around the body.Attempting difficult goals.Creating angle around defenders.Banana KickUsed to curve the football around an opponent.Generally reserved for experienced players.Checkside KickUseful when space or body position limits the use of a drop punt.Requires considerable practice.Torpedo PuntAlthough less common than in previous generations, the torpedo remains useful when maximum distance is required.Examples include:Defensive clearing kicks.Long kick-ins.End-of-quarter situations.Accuracy is generally reduced compared with the drop punt.1.4 Coaching PhilosophyThe drop punt should form the foundation of every player's kicking development.Young players should not spend excessive time practising advanced kicking techniques before developing a reliable drop punt.Strong fundamentals provide the platform for more advanced skills later.1.5 Teaching OrderPlayers should generally learn kicking in the following sequence:Stationary technique.↓Short targets.↓Moving targets.↓Kicking while moving.↓Passive pressure.↓Active pressure.↓Decision making.↓Game situations.Skipping stages often leads to inconsistent technique.1.6 Coaching CuesSimple coaching cues produce the best learning.Examples include:Eyes on the ball.Drop the ball onto the boot.Point your toe towards the target.Balance before power.Finish towards your target.Stay relaxed.Coaches should avoid introducing multiple cues simultaneously.1.7 Common Technical ErrorsBeginning players frequently:Throw the ball onto the boot.Drop the ball from too high.Lean backwards.Watch the target instead of the football.Swing across the body.Rush the kicking action.Each error should be corrected individually.Avoid overwhelming players with multiple technical changes at once.1.8 Age-Specific CoachingUnder 8Focus on enjoyment.Develop confidence.Encourage both feet.Do not emphasise distance.Under 10Improve consistency.Introduce moving targets.Encourage balance.Under 12Introduce pressure.Increase decision making.Develop kicking while moving.Under 14Introduce tactical kicking.Switching play.Forward entries.Defensive exits.Under 16 and AboveDevelop match execution.Pressure.Fatigue.Decision speed.Role-specific kicking.Practical ExampleA coach notices several players leaning backwards while kicking.Instead of correcting every aspect of their technique, the coach focuses on one instruction."Keep your chest over the football."After several repetitions, the players begin striking the ball more consistently.Only then does the coach introduce the next coaching point.Volunteer Coach ChecklistBefore teaching kicking:✓ Demonstrate the skill.✓ Explain why the skill matters.✓ Keep coaching cues simple.✓ Allow plenty of repetition.✓ Progress gradually.✓ Encourage both feet.✓ Praise good decisions as well as good technique.Common Coaching MistakesFocusing on distance instead of accuracy.Teaching advanced kicks too early.Giving too many coaching cues.Ignoring the player's non-preferred foot.Practising kicking without decision making.Correcting every mistake immediately.AI Decision RulesWhen recommending kicking drills:Begin with drop punt fundamentals.Match drill difficulty to player ability.Progress towards match realism.Encourage both left and right foot development.Increase decision making before increasing distance.Prioritise accuracy before power.Chapter SummaryKicking is the foundation of Australian Football.The most effective coaches understand that successful kicking combines sound technique, intelligent decision making and consistent execution under pressure.By developing players through a logical progression, coaches build footballers capable of using their kicking skills effectively in match situations.The following chapter introduces the complete AFCRL Kicking Drill Library, beginning with the most fundamental kicking activities before progressing to advanced match simulation drills.Next Chapter: drills.title: Testing and Assessment Chapter Final Assessment
drills.objective: Complete a final integrated assessment that verifies player performance across technical, physical, tactical and match demands while evaluating the reliability and practical value of the club’s testing system.

groundSize.description: Full oval, half-oval testing stations and a private player-review area.

time.raw: Two to three hours across one extended session or two separate sessions

setup: Review the complete Testing and Assessment chapter and select age- and role-appropriate measures.
Establish four assessment components:Technical skill verification.
Football-specific physical and movement testing.
Tactical and positional assessment.
Integrated match-performance simulation.
Assign trained staff to every testing and observation responsibility.
Calibrate all coaches before testing.
Prepare clear scoring, validity and modification rules.
Divide the squad into balanced testing groups.
Establish recovery periods and medical oversight.
Prepare video coverage and a central data-control point.
Ensure individual development plans and previous baseline results are available.
instructions: Players complete a standardised warm-up.
Each player completes selected technical assessments covering kicking, handballing, marking and ground-ball work.
Players complete role-appropriate movement assessments covering acceleration, agility, deceleration, repeat effort or aerial capability.
All raw results, test versions and modifications are recorded.
Players receive a recovery break.
The squad completes a tactical assessment covering role execution, field-position decisions or structured team phases.
Teams then complete an integrated match simulation.
Observers code possession quality, contested involvement, off-ball work, communication, transition and positional role execution.
Video is used to verify key actions and uncertain ratings.
Players complete a self-assessment after the practical session.
Coaches check all data before interpreting results.
Results are compared with previous baselines and appropriate role benchmarks.
Each player receives a review containing verified strengths and no more than two development priorities.
Individual development plans are updated.
Coaches review the reliability, efficiency and usefulness of every test used.
Tests that do not produce reliable or actionable information are modified or removed from future batteries.
coachingPoints: Use only tests appropriate to the players and purpose.
Standardise instructions, equipment and conditions.
Preserve raw data.
Record invalid and modified attempts clearly.
Separate decision quality from execution.
Interpret physical results with football performance.
Use multiple observations before reaching conclusions.
Avoid creating one overall player ranking.
Protect player privacy.
Convert every meaningful finding into a coaching or development action.
observations: Skill quality under fatigue or pressure.
Agreement between player and coach ratings.
Whether testing results match observed football performance.
Whether the assessment process produces useful training priorities.
Whether any test creates unnecessary load or limited practical value.

commonErrors.error: Every available test is included regardless of purpose.
commonErrors.correction: Select measures linked to age, role and development needs.

commonErrors.error: Players are ranked using one combined score.
commonErrors.correction: Report technical, physical, tactical and match categories separately.

commonErrors.error: Modified tests are compared directly with standard results.
commonErrors.correction: Identify modifications and use appropriate comparisons.

commonErrors.error: Coaches collect data without changing training.
commonErrors.correction: Assign practical actions to every confirmed priority.

commonErrors.error: One match period determines the final assessment.
commonErrors.correction: Use testing, training, video and repeated match evidence.

commonErrors.error: Players receive excessive negative feedback.
commonErrors.correction: Present verified strengths and no more than two priorities.

commonErrors.error: The testing system itself is never reviewed.
commonErrors.correction: Evaluate reliability, efficiency, safety and coaching usefulness.

progressions: Link testing with official match statistics and running data.
Create pathway, senior and masters testing batteries.
Use the complete system at pre-season, mid-season and post-season checkpoints.
regressions: Complete the assessment across multiple sessions.
Compare only with the player’s previous baseline.
successIndicators: Demonstrate identifiable technical, physical and tactical strengths.
Recognise one or two priority development areas.
Contribute to their updated development plan.
Understand the actions required before the next review.
Interpret results in role and match context.
Convert findings into individual and squad training priorities.
Review and improve the assessment system itself.
drills.matchApplication: The final assessment connects isolated skill tests, football-specific movement, tactical understanding and match behaviour. It ensures the Testing and Assessment chapter produces practical coaching decisions, reliable player feedback and measurable development rather than disconnected testing results.
